expectedText:
TENANT'S NOTICE OF INTENT TO VACATE
Prepared for Acme Properties, LLC · Jordan Lee

NOTICE OF INTENT TO VACATE — DETAILS
NOTICE OF INTENT TO VACATE. To: Acme Properties, LLC. From: Jordan Lee. Property: 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield, currently rented at $2,200 per month. Date of this notice: September 1, 2026. Tenant hereby gives notice of Tenant's intention to terminate the tenancy of the above property and to vacate and deliver possession no later than October 1, 2026. This notice is intended to satisfy any minimum notice period that applies to ending this tenancy by law or under the rental agreement. Tenant's forwarding address, for purposes of receiving the security deposit itemization and any deposit refund, is: 456 Oak Ave, Springfield.

TENANT'S DEFAULT 30-DAY NOTICE TO END A PERIODIC (MONTH-TO-MONTH) TENANCY
For a periodic tenancy — one with no specified end date, such as a month-to-month tenancy — California statute lets either party end it by giving at least 30 days' written notice, at any time, with rent due and payable through the termination date. This is a two-way default rule: a tenant ending the tenancy on the tenant's own initiative gives the same 30-day notice a landlord would give. The statute lets the parties shorten this by their own agreement, made when the tenancy was created, to as little as seven days. The notice may be served the same way an unlawful-detainer notice is served under a separate statute, or by certified or registered mail to the other party — and a tenant giving notice has one further option not available to a landlord: mailing (by certified or registered mail) or personally delivering a copy to the landlord's own agent, specifically the agent to whom the tenant has been paying rent for the month before the notice. Separately, a landlord or the landlord's agent may not charge a tenant a fee for serving, posting, or otherwise delivering this notice.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "provided, however, that as to tenancies from month to month either of the parties may terminate the same by giving at least 30 days' written notice thereof at any time and the rent shall be due and payable to and including the date of termination."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1946(a), California Civil Code, the two-way 30-day default notice for a periodic tenancy (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1946.)
  "The notice herein required shall be given in the manner prescribed in Section 1162 of the Code of Civil Procedure or by sending a copy by certified or registered mail addressed to the other party. In addition, the lessee may give the notice by sending a copy by certified or registered mail addressed to the agent of the lessor to whom the lessee has paid the rent for the month prior to the date of the notice or by delivering a copy to the agent personally."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1946(a), California Civil Code, the tenant's own alternative way of serving this notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1946.)
  "A landlord or its agent shall not charge a tenant a fee for serving, posting, or otherwise delivering any notice, as described in this section."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1946(b), California Civil Code, no fee may be charged to serve this notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1946.)
  "Except as provided in subdivision (b), the notices required by Sections 1161 and 1161a may be served by any of the following methods: (1) By delivering a copy to the tenant personally. (2) If he or she is absent from his or her place of residence, and from his or her usual place of business, by leaving a copy with some person of suitable age and discretion at either place, and sending a copy through the mail addressed to the tenant at his or her place of residence. (3) If such place of residence and business cannot be ascertained, or a person of suitable age or discretion there can not be found, then by affixing a copy in a conspicuous place on the property, and also delivering a copy to a person there residing, if such person can be found; and also sending a copy through the mail addressed to the tenant at the place where the property is situated. Service upon a subtenant may be made in the same manner."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1162(a), California Code of Civil Procedure, the general service methods incorporated by reference into Section 1946's notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1162.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California), used as real evidence of what notice a tenant ending a periodic tenancy must give under this state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's tenancy; default notice periods for ending a periodic tenancy vary by state, and some states use a different default length entirely. Three of the four citations below come from the same statutory section (Civil Code section 1946, subdivisions (a) and (b)); Code of Civil Procedure section 1162 is the only independently enacted source among them, and even that section is drawn in only by cross-reference — section 1162's own text says it governs the notices required by Code of Civil Procedure sections 1161 and 1161a (the unlawful-detainer notices), not section 1946 by its own terms; section 1946 separately borrows 'the manner prescribed in Section 1162' for its own periodic-tenancy notice, so this document treats section 1162 as incorporated authority for this purpose rather than a source that independently addresses this notice on its own terms. This document addresses only the statewide default period; it says nothing about any city or county's own rent-control or just-cause ordinance, and many California cities layer additional notice or documentation requirements on top of this statewide floor. Neither this statute nor any published California case this research located addresses whether a tenant may unilaterally rescind or withdraw a notice of intent to vacate once it has been validly given; this document does not state a rule on that question because none was found, and nothing here should be read to say rescission is either freely available or unavailable.

A FIXED-TERM LEASE THAT SIMPLY ENDS: NO STATUTORY NOTICE REQUIRED — UNLESS THE TENANT HOLDS OVER
California's periodic-tenancy notice statute, by its own text, applies only to 'a hiring of real property, for a term not specified by the parties' — that is, a periodic tenancy such as a month-to-month tenancy. A lease for a fixed term, with a stated start date and a stated end date, is not a hiring for a term left unspecified, so this statute's notice-to-terminate requirement does not apply to it: the tenancy simply ends on the date the lease itself states, without either party needing to give any additional written notice under this statute for the tenancy to end on time. That changes if the tenant remains in possession after the fixed term's stated end date and the landlord accepts rent for a further period: California law then presumes the parties have renewed the hiring on the same terms, for a period not exceeding one month if rent is paid monthly (and not exceeding one year in any case) — converting what had been a fixed-term tenancy into a periodic one going forward, at which point the 30-day notice requirement described elsewhere in this document would then govern ending it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A hiring of real property, for a term not specified by the parties, is deemed to be renewed as stated in Section 1945, at the end of the term implied by law unless one of the parties gives written notice to the other of that party's intention to terminate the same, at least as long before the expiration thereof as the term of the hiring itself, not exceeding 30 days"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1946(a), California Civil Code, the notice requirement is limited by its own text to a hiring for an unspecified term (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1946.)
  "If a lessee of real property remains in possession thereof after the expiration of the hiring, and the lessor accepts rent from him, the parties are presumed to have renewed the hiring on the same terms and for the same time, not exceeding one month when the rent is payable monthly, nor in any case one year."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1945, California Civil Code, the holdover presumption that converts a fixed-term tenancy into a periodic one (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1945.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California), used as real evidence of what this state's law requires (and does not require) for a fixed-term tenancy's own expiration — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's tenancy, and other states' rules on this point vary. This document addresses only the statewide statutory floor; a specific fixed-term lease's own text may separately require the tenant to give the landlord advance notice of an intent to vacate, or of an intent not to renew, as a matter of the parties' private agreement rather than statute — this document does not have that lease's specific language and does not attempt to evaluate it. The two citations below come from two separately enacted Civil Code sections (sections 1945 and 1946), not the same section restated twice.

CIVIL CODE § 1946.1: MOSTLY A LANDLORD-SIDE DUTY, WITH ONE NARROW TENANT ROLE
A separate statute, Civil Code section 1946.1, requires an owner of a residential dwelling (and, since a 2025 amendment, an owner leasing to a 'qualified commercial tenant') to give a longer notice than section 1946's default when the owner ends a periodic tenancy: at least 60 days, or 30 days if the tenant has occupied for less than a year. That extended notice duty runs to the landlord, as the party required to give it — it does not lengthen the period a tenant must give under section 1946 when the tenant is the one initiating the end of the tenancy. Section 1946.1 does give the tenant one narrow, secondary role: once a landlord has already given a notice to terminate under this section, the tenant may also give the tenant's own notice under this same section, provided the tenant's notice covers a period at least as long as the periodic tenancy's own term and proposes a termination date earlier than the landlord's. Outside that specific after-the-landlord's-notice scenario, a tenant ending a periodic tenancy on the tenant's own initiative gives the ordinary 30-day notice described elsewhere in this document under section 1946, not a notice under section 1946.1.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Notwithstanding Section 1946, a hiring of residential real property or commercial real property by a qualified commercial tenant for a term not specified by the parties, is deemed to be renewed as stated in Section 1945, at the end of the term implied by law unless one of the parties gives written notice to the other of the party's intention to terminate the tenancy, as provided in this section."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.1(a), California Civil Code, this section's scope — it supersedes Section 1946 for the tenancies it covers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1946.1.)
  "After an owner has given notice of the owner's intention to terminate the tenancy pursuant to this section, a tenant may also give notice of the tenant's intention to terminate the tenancy pursuant to this section, provided that the tenant's notice is for a period at least as long as the term of the periodic tenancy and the proposed date of termination occurs before the owner's proposed date of termination."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.1(e), California Civil Code, the tenant's narrow right to give a competing, earlier-dated notice after the landlord has already given one (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1946.1.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, and both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Civil Code section 1946.1, subdivisions (a) and (e)); no independent second source was used for this specific point. The surrounding landlord-side 60/30-day notice duty itself is separately sourced to this same section elsewhere in this project's corpus — the Commercial Lease Agreement document's commlease_notice_to_terminate clause already quotes section 1946.1(b)-(c) and (k)(4) for that duty and for the definition of 'qualified commercial tenant' — and this clause does not re-quote that material; it adds only the scope-defining subdivision (a) and the tenant-facing subdivision (e), which that other clause does not cover. Whether a specific tenancy is subject to section 1946.1's landlord-side duty at all, or is instead governed by a purely local rent-control or just-cause ordinance with its own notice rules, depends on facts (property type, tenant category, and any applicable city or county ordinance) this document does not evaluate.

WHAT GIVING THIS NOTICE TRIGGERS: THE LANDLORD'S SEPARATE PRE-MOVE-OUT INSPECTION DUTY
Separately from the notice requirements described elsewhere in this document, California law ties a landlord's duty to offer a pre-move-out inspection to the moment either party gives notice of an intention to end the tenancy (or, for a fixed-term lease, to a point before the lease term ends, notice or not). Once a tenant delivers a notice like this one, the landlord must, within a reasonable time afterward, notify the tenant in writing of the tenant's option to request that inspection and of the tenant's right to be present for it. The full mechanics of that inspection right — when it must occur, the 48-hour scheduling notice, and its effect on what the landlord can later deduct from the security deposit — are addressed elsewhere in this project's corpus (the Security Deposit Itemization document's pre-move-out inspection clause) and are not repeated here; this clause identifies only that giving this notice is the event, on the tenant's side, that starts that separate clock.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Within a reasonable time after notification of either party's intention to terminate the tenancy, or before the end of the lease term, the landlord shall notify the tenant in writing of the tenant's option to request an initial inspection and of the tenant's right to be present at the inspection."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(f)(1), California Civil Code, the landlord's duty triggered by a party's notice of intent to terminate (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Civil Code section 1950.5(f)(1)), used as real evidence of what a tenant's notice of intent to vacate triggers under this state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's tenancy, and not every state ties an inspection right to the giving of notice at all. This is a single statutory subsection; no additional independent source was found for this specific triggering point, and this document deliberately does not re-derive the inspection right's own substance, already sourced elsewhere in this project's corpus, in order to avoid duplicating that content.

TENANT SIGNATURE AND DECLARATION OF SERVICE
Signed: Jordan Lee, Tenant. Date: _______________.

Declaration of Service. This notice was served on Acme Properties, LLC on _______________ (date), by the following method (check one): ☐ personal delivery to the landlord; ☐ delivery to the landlord's agent, in the manner prescribed by Code of Civil Procedure section 1162; ☐ certified or registered mail addressed to the landlord; ☐ certified or registered mail addressed to the landlord's agent to whom Tenant has paid rent for the month before the date of this notice.

Served by: _______________ (name) Date: _______________
